#47152. UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (946 w)
📖 Baca

UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda.
  • The UK and the EU strategy to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.
  • A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda.

The UK and the EU strategy to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.

Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.

Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.

It has been revealed that burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He remarked: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”.

The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the newly introduced deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.

It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.

Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action proposal in June this year.

Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.

According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.

The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action proposal, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.”.

In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed intends to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs.

A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe, the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders.

It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK.

In a recent development, previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers.

Starmer scrapped a Tory strategy to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed.

Recent findings suggest that before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal.

Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson stated: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.”.

The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel.

But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system.

Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, mentioned: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.”.

In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, noted return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run.

“Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said.

“The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.”.

A Home Office spokesperson noted: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration.

“We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”.

Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.
  • Sources indicate that the case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement.
  • As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

Sources indicate that the case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven.".

As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected.".

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

In a recent development, however, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights.".

Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

Sources indicate that "That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he noted.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they mentioned.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view.".

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press.".

Scheele mentioned he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

Industry observers note that "We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

Industry observers note that "That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice.".

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

Best Buy sells Blu-rays online and in-store again

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Best Buy is selling Blu-rays directly through its website and in physical stores again after exiting Blu-ray and DVD sales in 2023.
  • Industry observers note that the Best Buy website’s movie section currently lists 15 Blu-rays (including one two-pack) that are “sold & shipped by Best Buy.” New titles available include The Odyssey (2026), Project Hail Mary (2026), Supergirl (2026), Super Mario Galaxy (2026), and Obsession (2025).
  • Industry observers note that most of the Blu-rays are available for purchase online and can be delivered to an address or picked up at a Best Buy store within a few days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Best Buy is selling Blu-rays directly through its website and in physical stores again after exiting Blu-ray and DVD sales in 2023.

Industry observers note that the Best Buy website’s movie section currently lists 15 Blu-rays (including one two-pack) that are “sold & shipped by Best Buy.” New titles available include The Odyssey (2026), Project Hail Mary (2026), Supergirl (2026), Super Mario Galaxy (2026), and Obsession (2025). Best Buy is also selling some older titles on Blu-ray, including It’s a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972).

Industry observers note that most of the Blu-rays are available for purchase online and can be delivered to an address or picked up at a Best Buy store within a few days. As of this writing, The Odyssey appears to be in stock at Best Buy stores, as it’s right now listed as available for pickup within as little as an hour.

Ars Technica reached out to Best Buy to ask whether customers can expect the store to continue selling Blu-rays moving forward.

In October 2023, Best Buy announced that it would stop selling Blu-rays and DVDs online and in stores starting in 2024.

According to recent reports, “To state the obvious, the way we watch movies and TV reveals is much different today than it was decades ago. Making this change gives us more space and opportunity to bring customers latest and innovative tech for them to explore, discover and enjoy,” a Best Buy spokesperson said in a statement issued at the time.

Last year, the Best Buy website started selling Blu-rays and DVDs from third parties via its online marketplace.

Numerous other companies have reduced or ended their Blu-ray and/or DVD businesses in recent years. Target, for instance, only sells the discs in stores during special occasions (like holidays or for massive releases) now. Disney outsourced its DVD and Blu-ray business to Sony, which subsequently stopped selling recordable Blu-rays to people, and DVD rental company Redbox went out of business.

That said, physical media, including Blu-rays and DVDs, still have a place in many people’s homes. Because digital copies of movies and shows can be plucked from online platforms and people’s libraries that were previously “purchased” (but truly only rented) without warning, enthusiasts continue relying on physical media. Enthusiasts also opt for physical copies of movies and shows for better picture and/or sound quality than what’s available digitally, as well as for bragging rights.

It has been revealed that overall, the sales of Blu-rays and DVDs in the US have been steadily declining, and annual consumer spending dropped 9.3 percent from 2024 to 2025, according to the Digital Entertainment Group (DEG). During this same time, however, consumer spending on 4K Blu-ray discs specifically increased 12 percent year over year, per DEG.

A resurgence in Blu-ray sales has been associated with the growth of collectible SteelBooks, which are Blu-rays sold in collectible steel boxes, and Gen Z, which, in some cases, are even turning to video rental stores for Blu-rays and DVDs.

“We’re seeing a lot of evidence, including at the Criterion Mobile Closet, that more young people are thinking about physical media in a different way,” Peter Becker, president of Criterion, which sells Blu-rays and DVDs online, told the Los Angeles Times in February. “In an age where so much is available to us on demand, it becomes increasingly important to us.”.

#47147. Breaking: Apple HomePod mini 2 review: A necessary, but underwhelming update

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1522 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Apple HomePod mini 2 review: A necessary, but underwhelming update

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I'd be willing to forgive you if you forgot about the fresh HomePod mini.
  • In a recent development, the most notable patch on the HomePod mini 2 is on the inside.
  • The recently updated assistant isn't all the S10 is helping with here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'd be willing to forgive you if you forgot about the fresh HomePod mini. The overhauled smart speaker played a supporting role at best during Apple's Welcome Home event last month, behind the HomeView, and probably, in some minds, behind the updated Apple TV 4K. Still, the manufacturer provides a few upgrades in the HomePod mini 2 ($149), ensuring that it's ready for Siri AI and the assistant's newfound ability to offer personalized context for your queries. The main problem? The speaker doesn't yet support the recently upgraded virtual assistant Apple spent years improving.

In a recent development, the most notable patch on the HomePod mini 2 is on the inside. Apple swapped in its S10 chip from the Apple Watch Series 10, kicking the nearly antique S5 silicon to the curb. For a Watch comparison, that's like going from a Series 5 or first-gen Watch SE, which debuted in 2019 and 2020 respectively, to the 2024 edition. It's a massive leap, and it's one Apple claims was necessary for the HomePod mini to work with Siri AI.

The recently updated assistant isn't all the S10 is helping with here. Apple indicates the component can run real-time music evaluation "to optimize dynamic range, loudness and acoustic performance," with a hand from "advanced computational analysis." When connected to the newly introduced fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, you can use four HomePod mini 2 speakers as a surround sound setup. That S10 chip helps the speakers recognize their positions in a room and adjust the lag, convey that info to Apple's streaming box, and audio levels accordingly.

I only have two HomePod mini 2s, so I wasn't able to test this configuration, but I did hear it during Apple's event in October. Even with that brief experience, I can tell you using two second-gen HomePods as the front speakers and two HomePod minis as the rears is a much better setup. The HomePod mini doesn't muster enough bass to be a great home theater speaker on its own, and those full-size HomePods bring the boom when an action scene demands it.

In a recent development, before now, you could send audio from a Mac to a HomePod mini, but Apple has expanded the functionality so that the second-gen model can serve as persistent default speakers. This means, in theory, they'll stay connected to your Mac as the primary output rather than just relying on a temporary AirPlay link. This allows you to use the HomePod mini 2, or a pair of them, for everything on your computer — from FaceTime calls to games — without having to think about connecting each app or session to the speaker(s).

The HomePod line has always had lights on the top, but they haven't really done much. Before now, the top touch panel would light up if audio was playing or display an animation when you chatted with Siri. With a newly introduced feature called Sound Glow, those lights now show hues that compliment a song's album artwork. The lights move in real time, reacting to the bass and treble in each tune. If you opt for a soundscape, Sound Glow reacts to that too, showing an animation that resembles the pitter patter of rain drops, for example. It isn't a game-changing feature, but it's a nice use of lighting that was barely utilized previously.

Lastly, there are the latest colors. The HomePod mini 2 comes in pink, green, blue, white and midnight (dark grey), with those first three coordinating well with Apple's iMac colors. That list means the manufacturer retired orange and yellow from the previous generation, both of which looked great in their time. As you can see, my review units are green, and I've enjoyed the pop of color they've added to my desk over the last few weeks.

Given that Apple saw fit to bestow a "2" on this HomePod mini, I expected some upgrades to overall sound quality to be in the mix. Unfortunately, I can't notice a difference between old and new models. Sometimes I think there's some variation, but it's not substantial enough that I'm sure, and it's not consistent across various musical styles. I do like the audio performance of the HomePod mini for its size, but it still has a sound profile of crisp highs and prominent mids offset by bass tone that lacks dynamics and depth. It's good enough for casual listening or background tunes, but not for anything more than that.

Sources indicate that despite the lack of Siri AI, I was hoping the S10 chip would provide a performance boost for the old Siri experience you have to settle for right now. However, the assistant's responses to basic questions took the same amount of time as they do on the first-gen model. To be clear, they're quick on both devices, I'm merely pointing out there's no difference in this regard. Just don't try to ask the old assistant to dive into Apple's core apps for you, or try to have an on-going conversation — neither request will bear any fruit.

Industry observers note that the biggest problem with the HomePod mini 2 right now is its biggest omission: Siri AI. The recently updated assistant isn't available on the speaker yet, and Apple hasn't provided a timeline for its arrival either. The upgraded HomePod mini is equipped to support the now-current-gen Siri, thanks to the S10 chip. However, you'll have to wait for Siri's newfound contextual awareness to dive into your Messages, Calendar and other apps on your iPhone or iPad. And to me, that's a huge miss for Apple on an overhauled smart speaker. You'll also have to wait for the more conversational chats with Siri as the HomePod mini 2 doesn't yet support those either.

Recent findings suggest that I like the idea of using a HomePod mini 2 or a stereo pair of them as a persistent computer speaker with a Mac, but it's not a great experience in practice. Any time you do anything — start a song, pause a song, skip tracks — there's a 1-2 second delay in the audio responding. The lights on the top of the speakers, including the Sound Glow effect, will stop shining immediately, but the audio has to catch up. There's also a slight delay between speakers if you're using a stereo pair, which sounds like every song has added reverb. For these reasons, I found the Mac speaker feature more frustrating than enjoyable, and I rapidly moved back to AirPlay over a nearby Sonos speaker for my productivity tunes. And I haven't even mentioned the fact that I can't get the persistent connection to stick with my MacBook Air either. I'm constantly reselecting the HomePod mini 2 as the audio output.

According to recent reports, another item that's disappointing is something else that's not here: a substantial overhaul. The original HomePod mini is six years old at this point, so I expected a much bigger redesign for the second-gen version (until the rumor mill squashed that). If you have a first-gen HomePod mini, you'll miss out on the updated Siri, whenever it arrives, and newly introduced features like Sound Glow and the home theater option. And if you're hoping to create a stereo pair, you'll need two of the same generation HomePod minis to do that; you can't pair a first-gen speaker with a second-gen model for that purpose.

Lastly, there's the price. The previous version was $99 before Apple raised it to $129 in June when the company hiked the prices on pretty much all of its hardware. Now, I'm well aware of the global economic factors at play, especially the AI-fueled cost increase on RAM and other components, but asking $50 more than the first-gen model for incremental updates is tough. Had Apple kept the price at the June rate, the HomePod mini 2 would be a much easier recommendation.

Recent findings suggest that it's baffling to me that Apple would announce an updated HomePod mini without support for the latest version of Siri ready to go. The speaker's primary use is a hands-free conduit to the firm's voice assistant, after all. The only decent conclusion I can come to is that Apple wanted to announce what it considered was a full suite of home products around the HomeView debut, and it felt like the Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini and a collection of smart home devices were the best way to do that. I would be interested to know what the hold up is, because the Apple Watch Series 10 supports Siri AI already, and those wearables are also running the same S10 chip as the HomePod mini 2. But, of course, Apple isn't talking specifics.

After spending a few weeks with the HomePod mini 2, I mostly wish Apple had just waited. At a higher price, this isn't as compelling as it used to be in terms of getting Siri in your home. And with Siri AI missing, and some of the fresh audio features proving to be unreliable, it's clear a bit more polish was needed here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

It has been revealed that “RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded. “Killed by women.”.

Recent findings suggest that in case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.

“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.

Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.

According to recent reports, the concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.).

Industry observers note that more frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, currently facing multiple rape charges, complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.

If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people, bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it. (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.).

Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI.

It’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering—GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.

According to recent reports, what’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The alleged foreign agent was discovered with two Russian passports and a forged American passport.

A Russian man has been arrested in California's Silicon Valley for allegedly attempting to spy on employees of a technology and defence firm that supports the Ukrainian military.

Igor D'iu is accused of acting as an agent of a foreign government to conduct a covert operation in Palo Alto, near San Francisco. The BBC understands that the firm targeted was Palantir Technologies.

D'iu is also charged with stalking employees and possessing falsified identity documents.

The company is not named in charging documents, but is described as a publicly traded technology and defence company that produces software used by Ukraine in its war with Russia.

"The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian.

"We will not tolerate any efforts - by foreign governments or otherwise - to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations.".

Prosecutors say that D'iu entered the US unlawfully via the Mexico border, after travelling there from Istanbul in June.

He was allegedly recruited through the Telegram encrypted messaging app. His handlers referred to Russia as "'the Motherland' and directed D'iu to gather information about the manufacturer because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine".

On their instruction, he purchased computers, phones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software - tools he needed for his spy mission.

He then went to a coffee shop located near the tech giant's offices in Palo Alto, where he photographed laptop screens of employees who were working there.

His handlers also allegedly "instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity".

The suspect allegedly took photos of employees screens at a cafe near the office.

A source in the industry confirmed that Palantir was targeted, and added that the operation did not penetrate the company's private systems.

They added that the organization has been "targeted extensively" by Russia over its involvement in Ukraine, and that the attacks are becoming "increasingly aggressive".

The source, who did not want to be named, noted that this was the first time a Russian operative was found while on US soil attempting to spy on the tech giant.

"I think the surprising thing is that they decided to take the risk of sending someone to the US," they said, in an attempt to get into the system "physically".

Palantir has not issued a statement in reaction to the charges.

D'iu also allegedly conducted surveillance of employees and their residences.

According to recent reports, on 3 September, he followed a vehicle driven by one senior executive for nearly 30 miles. He fled after she drove to a police station. Police later obtained evidence that he had followed other employees' cars on previous days.

During the investigation, officials discovered identity cards that had been falsified - including a US passport, California ID card, and a Social Security card with the fake name "Hugo Landry Johns".

A raid on his home in October in East Palo Alto turned up a handwritten notebook that contained numerous home addresses of employees "family members' names, educational and employment histories, and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses", prosecutors say. Two Russian passports were also found.

He faces two charges related his alleged work as a foreign agent, one charge of interstate stalking, and one count of fraud related to his identity documents. He faces over 15 years in prison if found guilty.

The suspect was found with forged identification documents including a US passport.

He has been held in jail since 2 November. It is unclear whether he has hired a lawyer who can speak on his behalf.

Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.

Breaking: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire.
  • British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a upcoming mobility scheme.
  • It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that EU students would pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire.

British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a upcoming mobility scheme.

It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that EU students would pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.

The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.

As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement on Friday.

The EU-UK reset talks went down “down to the wire”, sources said, as both sides battled over the nature of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules.

But on the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.

There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.

The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards but France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start.

Instead, the UK will be consulted on upcoming food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.

Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.

It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.

The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.

With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some central sticking points.

Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”.

A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.

Another EU diplomat mentioned ambassadors representing the EU member states would meet at 5pm and “will go until agreement is reached tonight”.

Sources said the UK was still resisting pressure from the EU on tuition fees for EU students coming to Britain under the youth mobility scheme.

Recent findings suggest that “We are fighting hard on this and think we will get there,” said an EU insider. “But for us, one of the hardest discussions centres on this question of the UK being a rule taker or rule maker.”.

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP, including the a highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.

The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 noted the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”.

According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting newly introduced SPS rules.

Industry observers note that an EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”.

Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.

A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.

In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.

“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they noted.

Industry observers note that the issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” noted a second EU diplomat.

The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.

The concern raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.

The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.

Separately, the EU and UK remain deadlocked over whether EU students in Britain should pay the British or international tuition fee rate.

The draft proposal gives the UK two options: to agree to significantly reduced undergraduate fees or equal treatment with nationals.

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.

“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement to language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.

Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.

“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that fiona, the beloved Cincinnati Zoo hippo who became an internet sensation after surviving a premature birth in 2017, has died at age 9. The zoo revealed Thursday that Fiona died after accidentally swallowing a knit hat that fell into her enclosure earlier this month, despite days of intensive veterinary care.

Her death has prompted an outpouring of grief online from fans who watched her grow from a vulnerable 29-pound newborn into one of the internet's most recognizable animal celebrities.

Born six weeks premature, Fiona became a viral sensation as the Cincinnati Zoo documented her unlikely survival on social media. Millions followed her progress, celebrating everything from her first steps to her swimming lessons. Nearly a decade later, she remained a beloved fixture of internet culture, inspiring memes, merchandise, and a devoted online following.

Nearly a decade later, the internet is mourning her loss. The Cincinnati Zoo confirmed her death in a heartbreaking statement, explaining that its veterinary team had spent days attempting to help Fiona pass the foreign object. Despite round-the-clock care and multiple treatments, her condition deteriorated.

"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement, as reported by the BBC. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore.".

Industry observers note that according to the zoo, the hat entered Fiona's habitat in a freak accident involving a visitor and a ceiling fan. The zoo consulted veterinary and medical specialists, but surgery was not considered a viable option for the full-grown hippo.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her," Jenike said. "They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore.".

Long before the internet fell in love with Moo Deng, there was Fiona.

When Fiona arrived on Jan. 24, 2017, she was the smallest premature hippo known to survive in human care. Unable to stand long enough to nurse from her mother, Bibi, she required intensive care from zoo staff, who worked alongside specialists from Cincinnati Children's Hospital to keep her alive.

Her recovery promptly became an online phenomenon. Through photos, videos, and regular updates from the Cincinnati Zoo, fans followed Fiona's earliest milestones, from learning to swim to growing strong enough to reunite with her family. The hashtag #TeamFiona became a rallying cry for people who had never visited Cincinnati but nevertheless felt invested in the little hippo's survival.

Sources indicate that she eventually inspired children's books, merchandise, memes, and even an ice cream flavor. Her birthday became an occasion for celebration, and visitors traveled from around the world to see her in person.

For the past nine years, Fiona has been a familiar presence in people's social media feeds, an unlikely celebrity whose fans have watched her grow from a vulnerable newborn into a playful, 2,000-pound hippo.

And unlike so many fleeting internet sensations, Fiona never really disappeared from the public's affection.

News of Fiona's death prompted an outpouring of grief across social media Thursday, with longtime fans sharing memories, photographs, and tributes to the hippo who had become a symbol of resilience.

For many, the circumstances of her death made the news especially difficult to process. Social media users expressed anger that an accidentally discarded object could have such devastating consequences, while others urged compassion and discouraged directing harassment toward the family involved.

In a recent development, the loss also resonated with Cincinnati residents, for whom Fiona had become something of an unofficial mascot. Her unlikely survival story was woven into the city's identity, and her life had been celebrated by generations of zoo visitors.

Recent findings suggest that "Fiona was such a gift," Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard said in a statement. "I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life.".

Fiona would have turned 10 in January.

Recent findings suggest that for an animal whose earliest days were shared with the world, her death feels unusually personal. Millions of people watched her learn to swim, celebrated her birthdays, and cheered as she grew into a healthy adult. They knew her story because they had been following it almost from the beginning.

The internet helped make Fiona famous. But it was her unlikely survival — and the joy she brought people along the way — that made her unforgettable.

Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core.
  • Industry observers note that STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance.
  • It has been revealed that the upcoming Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core. Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft claims is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency’s (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG).

Industry observers note that STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft notes that concern is now managed: “The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened.”.

It has been revealed that the upcoming Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.

According to recent reports, this isn’t to say that system administrators won’t still have the final say on which security protocols are activated, just that the default package now ships in a pre-hardened state. Kerberos is now the default over NTLM, with protections added to LSASS; TLS is automatically restricted to modern cipher suites; key exchange uses “hybrid post-quantum key exchange” based on the quantum-safe ML-KEM; and remote desktop authentication and PowerShell script block logging get stricter as well.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s native NVMe storage stack was originally introduced via an upgrade to Windows Server 2025, but it required administrators to enable it manually. The update eliminated NVMe translation through a SCSI stack while improving speeds and reducing overhead. The redesigned stack will now be default-on in Windows Server 2028.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft is upfront, noting that the new hardened security settings may break things due to software compatibility concerns with older protocols, legacy authentication, or management tools and scripts. The organization encourages users to try things and provide feedback about what goes wrong. “We want to hear where a hardened default gets in the way of a real workload: which setting, which application, and what you had to change to get it working,” the Windows Server Team stated in a blog post. “That is how the defaults get better before general availability.”.

Microsoft suggests that users use the preview build as a test bed to determine where challenges like compatibility still arise. This is not a release candidate build and shouldn’t be treated as such. Despite the latest security stance that comes with the preview build, hardware-backed protections like Secure Boot and DMA requirements won’t be enforced until a later preview build. Kerberos is now the default preference over NTLM, but NTLM blocking itself will still have to wait for a later preview release.

Beyond those limitations, the current build has a known glitch that cuts into its hardened goals. According to the release notes, “A race condition in the TLS hybrid key exchange implementation may cause the LSASS service to crash when hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server.” Microsoft recommends disabling hybrid-key exchange groups until the problem is addressed.

System administrators and curious homelabbers interested in testing the new Windows Server 2028 can do so by registering with the Microsoft Windows Insider Program.

    Google signs deal with Blue Origin to send satellite data centers into orbit

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This is part of Project Suncatcher, an experiment aimed at running AI systems in space.
    • Google has partnered up with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to deploy small satellite data centers into space, as part of its Project Suncatcher project.
    • The rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This is part of Project Suncatcher, an experiment aimed at running AI systems in space.

    Google has partnered up with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to deploy small satellite data centers into space, as part of its Project Suncatcher project. Each of these satellites will be equipped with "roughly the capacity of a data center rack" and will enter into a sun-synchronous orbit via heavy-lift Newly introduced Glenn rockets.

    The rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers. The first launch isn't scheduled until early 2029, so we have a couple of years to see if this whole project even works.

    In a recent development, blue Origin and Google have entered into a launch services agreement for Project Suncatcher, Google's research moonshot exploring how an interconnected network of solar-powered satellites equipped with its AI chips, Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), could scale machine learning... pic.twitter.com/dUWuHR4Pla.

    — Blue Origin (@blueorigin) November 19, 2026.

    This is an experiment that Google calls a "long-term moonshot" to see if it's possible to put AI infrastructure in space by "tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit." The benefits of this would be massive. Data centers here on Earth are notorious hogs, with their snouts all over electricity grids, land and cooling systems.

    The hope is that the harsh vacuum of the cosmos will be a better fit for the technology. After all, in space nobody can hear you make endless industrial noises and high-pitched whirs all day every day. This is a very real situation for folks living near data centers.

    Sources indicate that google is far from the only tech giant trying to kick the data center can straight into outer space. Elon Musk's SpaceX has been experimenting with the idea, though it may involve putting a gigantic catapult on the moon (really.) There are also some startups fiddling with the technology, like Starcloud.

    Sources indicate that can this even work? We don't know yet, though there are some serious hurdles to overcome. Google did deploy its first AI server satellite back in October, but it was sent into low-Earth orbit and can only operate for 15 minutes at a time. Scaling up the affiliated cooling systems looks to be incredibly difficult.

    Industry observers note that that's because standard heat dissipation doesn't work in space, so it has to be released through pipes and panels rather than conventional cooling systems. There's also the matter of radiation. It's everywhere and causes something called "bit flip." This essentially flips the binary code from a one to a zero, or vice versa. Obviously, this would be a major matter for binary-coded systems.

    In a recent development, did I mention the actual rolls out? It's extremely expensive to send stuff to space. Just one Falcon 9 launch costs around $74 million and the maximum payload can barely cover the hardware for a small server room, let alone a hyperscale data center.

    Sources indicate that "Expanding from one satellite to a vast network of them that operate like a giant data center will take years and enormous funds," Brandon Lucia, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, told The Fresh York Times. "If you do this on a large scale, there are additional engineering problems.".

    Finally, there's a risk to us humans here on Earth. Scientists have been considering a theoretical scenario called Kessler syndrome for decades. This is when the density of objects in low-orbit gets so high and collisions become so commonplace that it creates a chain reaction of debris. We would be on the receiving end of that debris.

    Industry observers note that this theory was posited back when there were just under 2,000 items circling a low-Earth orbit. That number has since risen to over 47,000 and Elon Musk recently floated an idea to add millions of new satellites into the mix.

    Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.

    Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.

    The stock opened at $111.50 — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the organization's valuation at $2 trillion.

    The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

    The San Francisco-based manufacturer behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.

    This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    According to recent reports, anthropic is the first massive AI manufacturer to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.

    Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.

    Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.

    That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

    Tech Report: How to game share GTA 6 and split the cost with a friend

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (406 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can do this on Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5.
    • Industry observers note that even if you've been eagerly awaiting the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, shelling out $80 for the standard edition or $100 for the ultimate edition isn't easy for everyone.
    • Sources indicate that both Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5 have a game sharing feature that lets you play one copy of a game on two different consoles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can do this on Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5.

    Industry observers note that even if you've been eagerly awaiting the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, shelling out $80 for the standard edition or $100 for the ultimate edition isn't easy for everyone. You shouldn't expect the biggest game of the year to go on sale any time soon, but the good news is there's another way to save some money on it. The only catch is that you need a friend who wants to play the game on the same kind of console and is willing to split the cost with you.

    Sources indicate that both Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5 have a game sharing feature that lets you play one copy of a game on two different consoles. While there are some restrictions on sharing DLC and other in-game items, most full games can be shared, and GTA 6 is no exception.

    On PlayStation 5, sharing works by signing into your account on two different consoles and enabling the console sharing feature. After buying GTA 6, sign into your PlayStation account on the console you want to share the game with. Open Settings on the console's main screen, then go to Customers and Accounts and select Other. Open Console Sharing and Offline Play and toggle the feature on.

    While logged into your account, your friend can now download any of your games to their own console, then switch back to their own account to play the game. Keep in mind that your account can only share games with one other console at a time. Your friend will also need to remember to switch back to their own account after starting to download one of your games, since you can't use the same account on two consoles simultaneously. Once you've set up console sharing, your friend will maintain access to your library permanently unless you change your password.

    Recent findings suggest that this will allow anyone using this Xbox to download games on your account without you signing in. In the menu itself, a note recommends making your own console your home Xbox, but that would only allow another user to play GTA 6 on your own console. Also note that you can only switch your home Xbox five times per year, so be mindful of that limit if you want to change who you're sharing games with.

    NEON has released a upcoming poster for Luca Guadagnino's upcoming OpenAI film Artificial, and the visual is peak uncanny valley.

    The illustrated poster centers on Andrew Garfield as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who stands in a redwood forest overlooking San Francisco Bay. He holds out a hand, inviting us into an unknown future.

    For anyone who's ever wanted to go hiking with Garfield, the image seems like a dream come true. But stare at the poster for more than one second, and your brain starts to reject everything that's in front of it. Why does that redwood have a face? Why is a grassy hill glitching into a tunnel? Why does Altman look like he's about to call me "Spider Monkey" and take me on a piggyback ride through the woods, Edward Cullen-style?

    Recent findings suggest that most importantly: Why does everything carry the discomforting sheen of AI? Could NEON have missed the point of Artificial's cautionary tale entirely and made promotional materials using AI?

    Don't panic. A line of text alongside the bottom right edge of the poster affirms that the artwork was made by humans. To back that affirmation up, NEON also released a video of the poster being digitally illustrated, tagging creative agency Gravillis Inc. and artist Mike Thompson.

    Comments under NEON's initial post of the poster appreciated the clever AI-adjacent marketing tactic.

    "Chefs kiss on the poster which was made by an artist satirizing the AI aesthetic we all know and (should) hate," one user wrote.

    "Poster meant to look like AI, but still has the humanity of an artist, so it’s still pretty to look at," wrote another.

    If you were still somehow on the fence about whether Artificial would be pro- or anti-AI, look no further than the poster's background, which highlights the Golden Gate Bridge partially submerged. Whatever future Garfield's Altman wants to bring us into, it's clearly calamitous.

    The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance mentioned it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.

    The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.

    “Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland remarked.

    “The government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”.

    Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.

    The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.

    “This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”.

    “It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”.

    The streaming wars, or the battle to be the top streaming organization, are ongoing, according to Ted Sarandos, a co-CEO of what many would consider today’s frontrunner.

    But in an interview with Bloomberg published today, Sarandos noted that people are still spending significant time watching traditional broadcast TV.

    “The streaming wars are continuing as we go. Half of television engagement in the United States is still linear, old television,” he stated, without specifying the source of the statistic. According to analysis from Nielsen, streaming represented 49.6 percent of TV viewing in August, with 36.4 percent coming from broadcast and cable. That still suggests a sizable amount of viewing time for streaming providers to target.

    As Netflix seeks to strengthen its lead against rivals like YouTube and Skydance, there’s extra pressure for it to deliver hit shows and movies.

    I think as Netflix has grown and matured and the business has grown and matured around us, that hit rate really matters. And you’ve got to get ahead of ‘are we on a path to continue [and] maintain that hit rate in the US particularly, but everywhere in the world?’ And I’d say the business is working everywhere in the world, including the US, but we should be doing better in the US than we were. And we’ve got to really focus on our ability to do that.

    The CEO remarked that Netflix is focusing on “the ambition of storytelling” rather than “chasing everything that people just happen to spend five seconds on television on” or relying on AI-generated content.

    “I think what’s going to happen is that people will desire more ambitious, more accomplished storytelling in a world that is flooded with slop,” Sarandos noted.

    According to recent reports, netflix has used generative AI-based workflows for various production tasks, like creating crowds or historical battle scenes, for hundreds of titles. This has helped Netflix save money while it increased the amount it spends on content this year by about 10 percent.

    When it comes to streaming people struggling to find something to watch, Sarandos acknowledged that Netflix sometimes “make[s] mistakes about how we present new things” and can “bury things that you might be looking for under new things that you’re not coming for.” He pointed to AI as a tool for content discovery in addition to aiding in the pre-production and post-production of content.

    Netflix is also being more open toward theater releases than it has been historically. That change was on the forefront when Netflix was trying to buy Warner Bros. Discovery’s (WBD’s) movie studios business (as well as its streaming business) and convince critics that the acquisition wouldn’t mean fewer theater releases. Although Netflix pulled out of the deal, it’s still eying an increase in theater releases as an opportunity. During the interview, Sarandos noted that the sequel to Netflix’s most popular movie of all time, KPop Demon Hunters (2025), “will be huge in theaters and massive on Netflix.” It has also mentioned that it will put movies in theaters for longer and recently extended the scheduled theater release for Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew from two weeks to seven.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1100 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a upcoming draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
    • The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
    • This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a upcoming draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

    The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.

    This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.

    The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.

    It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.

    The draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, remarked negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.

    Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.

    "This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he noted in a statement.

    Another hotly contested glitch at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.

    Industry observers note that the second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion). It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world.".

    "Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," mentioned Raman.

    The European Union has mentioned it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.

    The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.

    It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.".

    Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen noted the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand.".

    The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.

    The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.

    Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries noted the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community.".

    The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.

    Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.

    On Thursday, Panama noted it would block any agreement that does not meet its demand for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate the potent greenhouse gas methane.

    The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

    Australian Energy Minister Bowen stated he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.

    "We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a proposal we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming.".

    The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

    It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

    The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

    Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such asa Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.

    "It's critically vital for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," said David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

    • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
    • Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stories revealing Pauline Hanson’s US trip with Gina Rinehart and the systemic betrayal of Kardell Lomas before her death recognised.

    Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

    Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.

    Investigative reporter Sarah Martin won the award for print/text news report for her exclusive story that revealed the One Nation leader and her chief of staff, James Ashby, travelled with Rinehart on the mining magnate’s Gulfstream 700 on 27 October last year.

    The pair stayed at Rinehart’s Palm Beach mansion, close to US president Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.

    After Guardian Australia published details of Hanson’s flight, her office lodged an amendment to the registrar of senators’ interests declaring the sponsored travel.

    Queensland correspondent Ben Smee and the Guardian team won the award for coverage of Indigenous affairs for the story of the betrayal of Kardell Lomas, who repeatedly sought help – from domestic violence support services and the police – to escape the violent and dangerous man who killed her.

    Lomas had 24 interactions with various agencies – and she repeatedly disclosed fears for her safety, death threats, serious violence and other abuse.

    Nick McKenzie won the 2026 Gold Walkley, regarded as the highest honour in Australian journalism, for his investigation into Victorian underworld figure Mick Gatto, and how the state Labor government handled the $100bn infrastructure program, Massive Build.

    Sources indicate that walkley judges called it “truth-to-power journalism, in the face of attempts to shut him down with actual violence. It’s not just a Victorian story, it speaks to our nation and the way our democracy works. Tenacious reporting presented in accessible ways, instrumental in bringing down a government.”.

    Smee and Martin were also finalists in the long feature writing category, Martin for “Inside One Nation” and Smee for “‘Starting to frighten me’: the final weeks of Hannah Clarke’s life”.

    Guardian Australia’s business editor, Jonathan Barrett, was a finalist in the short feature writing category for his story “‘A child goes to bed and doesn’t wake up’: the families left in shock after the sudden death of their healthy children”.

    The 2026 Walkley print/text award for feature writing under 4,000 words was awarded to the Australian Financial Review’s Sam Buckingham-Jones for the story “Maccas in a Rolls: inside Kyle Sandilands’ pivot to $100 tradie plans”.

    For feature writing over 4,000 words, the Age and the Sydney Morning Herald’s Melissa Fyfe and Carla Hildebrandt took home the award for their story “Virginia: the Final Chapter”.

    The scoop of the year was awarded to the ABC team behind “Bondi: what ASIO knew”, which included Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop, Olivia Caisley and Michael Workman.

    Tony Wright, an associate editor and special writer for the Age and the Sydney Morning Herald, took home the award for outstanding contribution to journalism.
