    Elon Musk notes SpaceX has a plan to eliminate cell phone dead zones

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • CEO Elon Musk stated SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.
    • These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk mentioned, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.
    • “We’ve got a proposal that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the tech giant is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    CEO Elon Musk stated SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.

    These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk mentioned, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

    “We’ve got a proposal that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the tech giant is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”.

    The company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

    In a recent development, combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he noted. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”.

    Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”.

    The idea isn’t fresh, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.

    SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell stated during the firm’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.

    Even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

    Sources indicate that spaceX’s blueprint to build a hybrid celluar-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so because he expects an entirely fresh class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

    “I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he remarked, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (704 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits.
    • Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
    • In a recent development, the baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits.

    Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

    In a recent development, the baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

    The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

    Sources indicate that the case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

    The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

    Recent findings suggest that otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, mentioned: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”.

    According to recent reports, sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, mentioned she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted swiftly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

    “As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their fresh leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she mentioned.

    The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

    Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

    “A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” mentioned Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”.

    Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

    Recent findings suggest that the trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”.

    Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

    The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” remarked Venter.

    A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping tech giant allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
